youtube_title: X-Men Toys Were Ruled 'Not Human' — to Cut Import Duty 🦝⚖️
caption: In Toy Biz v. United States (2003), the trade court held X-Men figures weren't 'dolls representing only human beings' because of non-human features — putting them in a lower-duty toy category under the tariff schedule of the time.
script: Marvel's own toy company went to court to prove the X-Men aren't human. And it won. [disclaimer] Yep. This really happened! It was a trade court case in America, back in two thousand three. Here's the deal. When you bring toys into the country, you pay a tax at the border. And back then, the tax depended on the kind of toy. Dolls that look like humans? Twelve percent. But toys that look like animals, monsters or robots? Only about seven percent. Big difference! So customs looked at the X-Men toys and said, these are dolls. Pay the big tax. But the toy company, Toy Biz, said, wait a second. Look closer! These are mutants! Wolverine has claws! Some of them have fangs. Some have tentacles. That's not human! And the court agreed. It said even one non-human thing, like claws, can keep a toy out of the doll group. So the X-Men got the cheaper tax. A company basically argued its own superheroes aren't people. And it worked! But not every toy won. One toy in the same case still counted as a doll. Here's the limit. This was only about toys and the old border tax rules. By the time of this case, those toy taxes had already been dropped for new imports. And it says nothing about whether anyone is actually human. [loop] So the next time someone calls your action figure a doll, remember
